Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

vignette:
Maya was thirty-seven years old, a guitarist who had spent nearly two decades weaving herself into the fabric of the local music scene. She still remembered the exact sound of the first blast-a crack that seemed to split the air inside the club, followed by a second, deeper thud that shook the floor under her feet. It was a small venue, the kind where the stage was barely elevated and the crowd stood close enough to touch the monitors. She had been between sets, standing at the bar, when the first explosion sent glass and splinters across the room. The taste came immediately: a sharp, acrid mix of smoke and metal, with something sweet underneath that she later learned was the residue of the explosive. That taste had stayed lodged in her memory like a piece of gravel, and it returned without warning now, months afterward-in the middle of a quiet dinner, or when she opened an oven, or when the air grew heavy with summer humidity. At those moments the whole scene would crash back: the flash, the screams, the weight of bodies pressing toward the exit, the strange stillness afterward when she found herself kneeling on the sticky floor, her ears ringing.

In the weeks that followed, Maya's mind refused to let the memory settle. It stayed too clear, too detailed-every edge of the broken glass, every note of the song that had been playing just before, the exact pressure of a stranger's hand on her shoulder as they pushed past. And sometimes, without any warning at all, it was as if she were right back there. She would be standing in her kitchen and suddenly she was on her knees again, heart hammering, convinced she could hear the second blast about to come. Her body acted before she could stop it-she would drop whatever she was holding, or crouch behind the counter, or snap at her partner for walking up behind her too quietly. She knew it wasn't happening, but knowing did not stop the surge of terror or the way her hands would shake for half an hour afterward.

The taste was the worst, because it was unpredictable. A whiff of something burnt on the stove, the metallic tang of a coin in her mouth, even the sweetness of certain perfumes-each could summon the whole memory in a flash. She had started to avoid cooking anything that might produce smoke, and she had thrown out several bottles of sauce that reminded her, in some way she could not name, of that night. But no amount of avoidance could keep the taste from appearing. It came in dreams, too, leaving her jolting awake, her mouth dry and sour.

Concentration became a daily battle. Maya had always been able to lose herself in a practice session for hours, working out a tricky chord progression or fine-tuning a solo. Now she could barely sit with her guitar for ten minutes before her mind skittered away. She would find herself staring at the fretboard, the notes blurring, a low-grade irritability building in her chest until she snapped at no one in particular. Her playing felt hollow, and she stopped accepting gigs because the thought of standing on a stage, surrounded by a crowd, was unbearable. The sounds of a live room-the shuffle of feet, the hum of amplifiers, the clink of glasses-now felt threatening. She had begun to see danger everywhere: a stranger who stood too close at the grocery store, a sudden laugh behind her, the way certain smiles did not quite reach the eyes. She had come to believe that people were not what they seemed, that the attack had revealed a hidden truth about the world: anyone could be a threat, and she could no longer tell the difference between safe and unsafe. That conviction crept into her relationship, too. She found herself scrutinizing her partner's moods, reading unease into pauses, flinching at unexpected touches. She had started sleeping in the living room, telling herself it was because she did not want to wake him with her nightmares, but really she felt a strange, shapeless distrust that made closeness feel like a trap.

The sense of belonging that had once anchored her-the community of musicians, the late-night jam sessions, the easy camaraderie of people who understood the language of rhythm and melody-had evaporated. She no longer belonged anywhere, not in the scene, not in her own home, not even in her own body. When she tried to imagine the future, she saw only a flat, gray stretch of years, empty of the music that had once defined her. It was not that she thought she would die soon; it was that she did not believe there was anything worth living toward.

What finally brought Maya to seek help was a small, trivial thing. She was in the waiting room of a doctor's office, and a child a few seats away unwrapped a lollipop. The sweet, fruity scent hit her nostrils, and suddenly she was tasting the metallic-sweet residue of that night again, her pulse roaring in her ears, her hands gripping the armrests so hard her knuckles went white. She excused herself, walked out into the parking lot, and sat in her car for twenty minutes, shaking. That night she told her partner she needed to talk to someone. She was not sure what she hoped for-only that she could not keep living like this, caught between a past that would not stay in the past and a future that felt like nothing.
